security.meta.title: Security & Privacy - encrypt.click
security.meta.description: How encrypt.click handles data: browser-side crypto, encrypted chat and transfers, what third parties see, and what we do not collect.
security.subtitle: A plain-language summary of how encrypt.click is designed to handle your data. For information only - not legal advice.
security.noAccounts.title: No accounts, no logins
security.noAccounts.text: encrypt.click has no user accounts, logins, or profiles. You do not need to register or provide personal information to use the tools.
security.clientSide.title: Browser-side tools
security.clientSide.p1: The privacy tools, such as AES words, Time capsule, Steganography, Photo cipher and Spectral cipher, run in your browser using Web Crypto and other browser APIs. Their inputs are not uploaded to encrypt.click for processing.
security.clientSide.p2: When a tool requests public data at your direction, such as drand randomness for Time Capsule through our same-origin proxy, the request does not include your plaintext secrets or passwords.
security.shortening.title: Link shortening
security.shortening.p1: After encryption, your browser sends the share link to /api/shorten on encrypt.click, which shortens it with our own service at l.encrypt.click. No third-party shorteners are used. If shortening fails, you get the full link instead.
security.shortening.p2: The short link stores the full link including the encrypted payload, but never the password. Anyone with the short link still needs the password, so use the generated passphrase or another strong password.
security.shortening.p3: The short link is created automatically, so the encrypted payload of every share is stored on l.encrypt.click, whichever link you end up sharing. The full link itself carries the payload in the URL fragment, which the recipient's browser never sends to a server.
security.cookies.title: Cookies and browser storage
security.cookies.p1: The site sets one functional cookie, ec-lang, only after you pick a language in the menu. It holds the two-letter language code, nothing else, for one year, and is not used for tracking. The first visit without it is served in your browser language. Your browser may use localStorage for the theme and, where chat history is kept, encrypted messages, in saved rooms also how far each member's history has been checked. Session storage may briefly hold a room password while you join, and keeps a room key that arrived in a link for as long as that tab is open, so the key can leave the address bar. IndexedDB holds the signing key your browser creates for each chat room and whiteboard and, for saved rooms, the seed of the post-quantum signing key, sealed under a key derived from the room link; the private keys never leave the device.
security.cookies.p2: Cloudflare (hosting) may set cookies for security and abuse prevention depending on traffic and browser settings, under Cloudflare's own policies.
security.network.title: Network and transport security
security.network.li1: All traffic is served over HTTPS with modern TLS.
security.network.li2: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) is enabled with includeSubDomains and preload.
security.network.li3: Content Security Policy (CSP) restricts scripts, styles, fonts, and connections; inline script hashes are used instead of broad unsafe-inline for scripts.
security.network.li4: Framing is disabled via frame-ancestors 'none' and X-Frame-Options: DENY.
security.thirdParty.title: Third-party infrastructure
security.thirdParty.p1: The site runs on Cloudflare Workers. Real-time chat and the whiteboard are relayed by Durable Objects in the same Worker (PartyServer). Calls may be relayed through Cloudflare TURN or another configured TURN provider. Temporary ciphertext hosts, including Send-compatible instances, may receive encrypted blobs when first-party upload is unavailable.
security.thirdParty.p2: encrypt.click does not maintain a database of your tool inputs. API abuse controls use a salted hash of the IP address held in memory for about 60 seconds. Cloudflare may also apply bot detection or challenges under its own policies.
security.disclosure.title: Responsible disclosure
security.disclosure.text: If you believe you found a security or privacy issue in encrypt.click, email mail@encrypt.click. Include enough detail to reproduce the issue and avoid testing that could impact other users.
security.nonLegal.title: Non-legal summary
security.nonLegal.text: This page is a human-readable summary of how encrypt.click is designed to handle data. It is not a contract or a complete set of legal terms. Perfect security cannot be guaranteed; you use the tools at your own risk.

tools.about.title: How it works
tools.aesWords.about.1.title: What it does
tools.aesWords.about.1: AES words encrypts a message with a password and then writes the encrypted bytes out as a list of words instead of an unreadable string of letters and symbols. The words are easier to copy by hand, dictate over the phone or paste into places that mangle special characters. Paste the same words back in with the same password and you get the original message.
tools.aesWords.about.2.title: The encryption
tools.aesWords.about.2: Your password and a random 16-byte salt go through Argon2id, the winner of the 2015 Password Hashing Competition, with 64 MiB of memory and 3 passes, and HKDF-SHA256 splits the result into a 256-bit key and a key commitment. The message is padded to one of a limited set of sizes so that its exact length does not show, then encrypted with AES-256-GCM and a random 12-byte nonce. AES (originally called Rijndael, designed by the Belgian cryptographers Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen) won a public NIST competition in 2000 and has protected everything from banking to TLS since. GCM mode also authenticates the data and the commitment ties the ciphertext to a single password, so a wrong password or a single changed word makes decryption fail instead of producing garbage.
tools.aesWords.about.3.title: Bytes to words
tools.aesWords.about.3: The encrypted result is split into 14-bit pieces and each piece picks one word from a fixed list of exactly 16,384 Czech words. The idea is old: the PGP word list from 1995 read key fingerprints aloud as words, and Bitcoin wallets use BIP-39 phrases with 2,048 words. Expect at least 55 words even for a very short message, because the header with the key derivation settings, salt, nonce and key commitment always travels along, together with the authentication tag.
tools.aesWords.about.4.title: Good to know
tools.aesWords.about.4: Everything runs in your browser and nothing is sent to encrypt.click. The words are ciphertext, not a password, so anyone who sees them can try to guess your password offline. Argon2id makes every guess cost 64 MiB of memory and noticeable time, which also slows down graphics cards and dedicated hardware, but a short or common password can still fall, so use a long passphrase. Words must match exactly, including Czech diacritics such as ě or ř, and their order matters.
tools.aesWords.about.5.title: Chat style
tools.aesWords.about.5: Chat style turns the same encrypted bytes into text that reads like a casual Czech chat message, with typos, missing accents and loose punctuation. The words come from a small statistical model of about 3,000 chat words, and the next bits of the ciphertext choose each word. Typos, accents, capitals and punctuation carry no data, so the text still decodes after they change. Expect around 200 words even for a short message, because the header, salt, nonce, key commitment and tag always travel with it. It looks like a chat to a casual reader, but it will not hide the fact that the text is generated from anyone who knows how the tool works.
tools.photoCipher.about.1.title: What it does
tools.photoCipher.about.1: Photo cipher hides an encrypted message inside an ordinary photo in a way designed to survive moderate JPEG recompression, which is what chat apps and social networks do to images. The person who receives the photo opens it here with the same password and gets the message back.
tools.photoCipher.about.2.title: How the message is hidden
tools.photoCipher.about.2: The photo is split into 8×8 pixel blocks, the same grid JPEG works on. Each block carries one bit by nudging its average brightness to the nearest even or odd step on a scale of 24 levels, a technique called quantization index modulation that Brian Chen and Gregory Wornell described around 1998. JPEG compression keeps the average brightness of a block quite well, so the bits tend to survive. Every bit is written 7 times in blocks spread across the picture, and a majority vote corrects damaged copies.
tools.photoCipher.about.3.title: Encryption and capacity
tools.photoCipher.about.3: Before hiding, the message is encrypted with AES-256-GCM using a key derived from your password with Argon2id (64 MiB of memory, 3 passes). The photo is scaled so that its sides are between 800 and 2,048 pixels. Capacity is small: an 800×800 photo holds roughly 78 characters, and larger photos hold more.
tools.photoCipher.about.4.title: Limits
tools.photoCipher.about.4: Resizing, cropping, filters, brightness changes or very strong compression destroy the hidden data, and some apps downscale large photos automatically. Send the photo as a file when you can and test it first. The brightness changes may show up as faint blockiness on smooth areas such as sky. The hiding pattern is public, so anyone with this tool can tell that a photo carries data; only the content is protected, by your password. Everything runs in your browser and the photo is not uploaded.
tools.spectralCipher.about.1.title: What it does
tools.spectralCipher.about.1: Spectral cipher draws a picture into sound. It turns an image into a WAV file that sounds like noise, but when you open the audio in a spectrogram viewer, which plots frequencies over time, the picture appears. The reveal mode does the reverse and extracts the image from such a WAV file.
tools.spectralCipher.about.2.title: A musical trick
tools.spectralCipher.about.2: Musicians have hidden images in spectrograms for decades. Aphex Twin put his own grinning face into a track on the 1999 Windowlicker single, Nine Inch Nails hid images in the Year Zero album in 2007, and Mick Gordon tucked pentagrams and the number 666 into the 2016 Doom soundtrack.
tools.spectralCipher.about.3.title: How it works
tools.spectralCipher.about.3: The image is resized to 512×512 pixels and turned to grayscale. Each column becomes a short slice of sound of about 46 ms, and each row becomes a frequency between 300 Hz and 14 kHz whose loudness follows the brightness of the pixel. The result, about 24 seconds long, is mixed into a carrier track; the strength slider sets how strongly the image stands out against it.
tools.spectralCipher.about.4.title: Good to know
tools.spectralCipher.about.4: This is a hidden picture, not encryption. There is no password, and anyone who opens the file in a spectrogram viewer such as Audacity will see the image. Use it for puzzles, art and fun, not for secrets. MP3 and AAC compression, resampling or trimming the start can blur or shift the image, so share the WAV as it is. Everything runs in your browser.
tools.steganography.about.1.title: What it does
tools.steganography.about.1: This tool hides an encrypted message inside a PNG image. The picture looks the same to the eye, but someone with the password can pull the message back out here. It is handy when you want a secret to travel as an innocent-looking image.
tools.steganography.about.2.title: An ancient idea
tools.steganography.about.2: Steganography means covered writing in Greek. Herodotus tells of Histiaeus, who around 500 BC shaved a slave's head, tattooed a message on the scalp and sent him off once the hair had grown back. The German abbot Johannes Trithemius gave the craft its name in his book Steganographia, written in 1499. Invisible ink and microdots continued the tradition, and digital images are its modern form.
tools.steganography.about.3.title: How it works
tools.steganography.about.3: The message is first encrypted with AES-256-GCM, with a key derived from your password with Argon2id (64 MiB of memory, 3 passes). The encrypted bits are then written into the least significant bit of the red, green and blue values of each pixel, starting at the top left. Changing a colour value by one out of 255 is invisible. Each pixel holds 3 bits, so even a small image can carry a long message.
tools.steganography.about.4.title: Limits
tools.steganography.about.4: The hidden data survives only an exact copy of the PNG file. Any resizing, cropping, editing or conversion to JPEG, which most chat apps and social networks do, wipes it out; send the file as a document or attachment, or use Photo cipher instead. The method is simple, and statistical tools can detect that an image carries data, even though they cannot read it without the password. Everything runs in your browser and nothing is uploaded.
tools.timeCapsule.about.1.title: What it does
tools.timeCapsule.about.1: Time capsule locks a message until a moment you choose. Before that time nobody can open it: not the recipient, not you and not encrypt.click. Afterwards, anyone with the capsule can. It suits sealed predictions, delayed reveals, contest answers or a letter to your future self.
tools.timeCapsule.about.2.title: drand and the League of Entropy
tools.timeCapsule.about.2: The lock is opened by drand, a public randomness beacon that grew out of research at the Swiss university EPFL. Since 2019 it has been run by the League of Entropy, a group of independent organisations that agreed to operate it together. Founders included Cloudflare, Protocol Labs, Kudelski Security, the University of Chile and EPFL, and today the network includes the Ethereum Foundation, University College London and more than a dozen others. Every 3 seconds the members jointly produce a threshold BLS signature for the next round number. No single member, and no small group of them, can create it alone or ahead of time.
tools.timeCapsule.about.3.title: How the lock works
tools.timeCapsule.about.3: Your chosen time is converted to a future drand round. The message is encrypted in your browser with tlock, a scheme published by drand researchers in 2023: identity-based encryption on the BLS12-381 curve, where the round number is the identity and the beacon's future signature for that round is the only key that opens it. Inside, the message is packed in the age format and sealed with ChaCha20-Poly1305. Encrypting needs nothing secret from anyone; decrypting needs the signature, which does not exist until the round arrives.
tools.timeCapsule.about.4.title: A short history of timelocks
tools.timeCapsule.about.4: Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and David Wagner proposed time-lock puzzles in 1996: problems that take a known amount of sequential computing to solve. Rivest's LCS35 puzzle, set at MIT in 1999 and expected to take 35 years, was cracked in 2019 by the Belgian programmer Bernard Fabrot after three and a half years of computing on a home PC. Puzzles like that depend on how fast computers get. tlock depends on a clock run by many organisations instead, so the unlock time is accurate to a few seconds.
tools.timeCapsule.about.5.title: Good to know
tools.timeCapsule.about.5: There is no password. After the unlock time, anyone with the capsule can read it, and the unlock time itself is visible inside the capsule. Your browser reaches drand through encrypt.click's server, which forwards requests to api.drand.sh. It sees which round is requested, never your message, and your browser checks every beacon's signature, so the server cannot fake one. If drand shut down before your round, the capsule could never be opened. Opening early would require a large share of the League's members to collude. The scheme is not resistant to future quantum computers.
chat.about.1.title: How to start
chat.about.1: Choose how messages are kept, pick a room name, set a password of at least 16 characters that is hard to guess and share the link with the people you want to talk to. Rooms are created only here, so every room gets a strong password and an explicit message mode; opening the address of a room that does not exist leads back to this form. The link does not carry the key: everyone has to type the password, which you should share another way, for example in person or over a different app. A saved room has no password: it gets a random address and a random 256-bit key after the # in its link, so that link is the key and must be shared just as carefully.
chat.about.2.title: Messages
chat.about.2: Every message is encrypted in your browser with AES-256-GCM. When you join, the password goes through Argon2id once, with 64 MiB of memory and 3 passes, so every offline guess is slow and memory-hungry. HKDF-SHA256 then splits the result into the message key, which also depends on the room's message mode, and a second, separate value that only proves to the server that you belong in the room. The server learns that value, never the encryption key, and the room on the server is named after a hash of it rather than after your room name. A saved room skips the slow password hash: its key is already random, so HKDF-SHA256 derives the message key and the access value from it directly. In rooms without server history each message also gets a second layer with forward secrecy, described below.
chat.about.3.title: What the server sees and keeps
chat.about.3: Rooms run on Cloudflare Workers. The relay forwards encrypted messages to the people in the room and does not store them, except in saved rooms, where it keeps the encrypted messages, at most 1000 per room, in the European Union until a member deletes the room or nobody has visited it for 90 days. Otherwise it keeps only the room settings, and deletes them when the room has been empty for 7 days. It does see when messages are sent, how many people are connected and, from the timing, when someone is probably typing. Every message is padded to one of a limited set of sizes, at least 512 bytes, so short messages, typing indicators and presence signals all look the same and longer ones only show their rough size. Cloudflare, like any host, sees your IP address, and the room name appears in the page address you load. In saved rooms it also keeps each member's public ML-DSA key, encrypted under the room key, so it cannot recognise a returning member by their key.
chat.about.4.title: History and disappearing messages
chat.about.4: In the default mode each participant keeps the history in their own browser: the signed messages, sealed under a key derived from the room secret, so they survive a reload. Members who are online hand up to the last 200 messages to a newcomer, encrypted for that newcomer alone and still carrying every author's signature, so nobody can put words in someone else's mouth while passing history on. Forward secrecy protects what crosses the relay; what members' browsers keep, they can show anyone who joins with the password, which is what this mode is for. In a saved room the encrypted history lives on the server instead, so it is there after a reload, on a new device or for someone who joins later; your browser keeps a copy too and asks the server only for what it has missed. You can instead make all messages disappear between 5 seconds and a day after they are shown, and then nothing is kept. In any room, ending a single message with !N, such as !30, makes just that message disappear after N seconds, and it is left out of the stored history. The timer runs in each participant's browser, so a modified client or a simple screenshot can still keep a copy.
chat.about.5.title: Calls
chat.about.5: Voice and video calls use WebRTC. On top of its standard DTLS-SRTP encryption, your browser encrypts every audio and video frame, screen sharing included, with AES-256-GCM before it leaves, in the style of SFrame. Each participant creates a random media key on joining and gives it to every other participant separately: inside the encrypted room channel, sealed once more with a key only those two browsers share for this call (ECDH P-256). When someone leaves, everyone who stays switches to a new key, so whoever left cannot decrypt what follows. Frames that do not decrypt are dropped, never played, and a browser that cannot encrypt frames cannot join a call. Call setup travels through the room as encrypted messages. Media always goes through a TURN relay, so participants never see each other's IP addresses; the relay only forwards encrypted packets. Every participant connects to every other one, so calls work best in small groups.
chat.about.6.title: Files
chat.about.6: Files up to 90 MB are encrypted in your browser with a random key of their own, including the file name. The key and the download link travel only inside the encrypted message, so a file is protected exactly like the message that carries it, forward secrecy included. The encrypted file is uploaded to encrypt.click's own storage, or, if that fails, to backup hosts through encrypt.click's server (files up to 50 MB only). The hosts see only the encrypted file, its size and the uploading address. Uploaded files are deleted 24 hours after upload; the message stays in the history, the download does not.
chat.about.7.title: Good to know
chat.about.7: The chat is only as private as the link or password: anyone who has it can join and read along from then on. In rooms with forward secrecy, though, a password learned later does not open traffic recorded before, although in the default mode members who are online pass recent history on to whoever joins. A wrong password leads to a room that does not exist, so if the page says the room does not exist although you expected others there, check the password. Up to 32 people can join a room.
chat.about.8.title: Member keys in saved rooms
chat.about.8: In every room your browser creates a signing key for that room and keeps it to itself; every message carries the public half and a signature, and anything unsigned is dropped, including history that other members pass on. Names are only labels: the random alias or whatever a member typed. Other members remember which key a name first appeared with and warn you when the same name, or one that only looks like it, shows up under a new key, which is what an impostor who knows the password or link would look like. The members panel shows a key code for each member, a short fingerprint of that one key, and a safety number derived from both your keys, which is the same on both screens: compare it in person or by voice. In a saved room a member's key is the pair of its Ed25519 and ML-DSA-44 keys, and the key code and the safety number cover both. A new browser or device gets a new key, so expect that warning after you switch. The signature proves who in the room wrote a message, not who they are, and the password or link is still the only thing that lets someone in. The message mode is part of the room key, so the server cannot quietly turn a room with disappearing messages into one that keeps history. In a saved room, whoever has seen the link can read everything for as long as the room exists, so share it with care and delete the room when it has served its purpose; deleting removes the history from the server and from the browsers of everyone connected.
chat.about.9.title: Forward secrecy
chat.about.9: In rooms that keep history only in browsers and in rooms with disappearing messages, the room key alone opens no message. Each browser creates a fresh P-256 key pair when it joins and keeps it in memory only. Every member has its own sending chain: each message is encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key that HKDF-SHA256 derives from the chain, then the chain moves one step on and used keys are deleted. Every other member gets the current chain key separately, sealed under a key made from their two ephemeral keys (ECDH) together with a secret derived from the room password, inside the signed room channel as always. Someone who records the traffic and learns the password later cannot read the messages without breaking the key exchange, and once the session is over the keys needed are on no device any more. A future quantum computer that breaks P-256 would still need the password; against someone who has both the password and such a computer, forward secrecy does not hold. Chains are replaced after 100 messages or 10 minutes and whenever someone leaves: the new chain goes only to members who answer, so whoever left cannot read on with the keys they had. Newcomers get each chain only at its current step, so nothing that crossed the relay before they arrived opens with their keys. Saved rooms have no forward secrecy: their history has to stay readable on any device that has the link.
chat.about.10.title: Saved rooms: complete history and post-quantum signatures
chat.about.10: Saved rooms check instead that their history is complete. Every stored message carries its author's running number and the hash of that author's previous stored message, both under the signatures. Your browser follows each author's chain as history arrives and remembers how far it got, and members who are online announce their latest number and hash. If the server leaves out messages, puts an author's messages in a different order or holds back the latest ones, or if two different messages claim the same place, the chat shows a warning. The server still deletes the oldest messages once a room holds 1000, and the chat points it out when that happened while you were away; it can also hold back the latest messages of someone who is not online, and the order between different authors is not checked. Saved rooms also sign every message with ML-DSA-44 (FIPS 204) next to Ed25519, and a message counts only if both signatures are valid, so forging one would take breaking both. Each browser keeps its ML-DSA key sealed under a key derived from the room link. Messages name that key by its hash, and the server keeps the members' public keys encrypted under the room key, so messages from members who are offline can still be checked. A message without a valid ML-DSA signature, including one whose ML-DSA key is not available, is dropped.
chat.roomMissingDetail: Either it has not been created yet or it expired, or the password is different. New rooms are created only through the create form, so they always get a strong password and an explicit message mode.
chat.configChanged: The room settings do not match
chat.configChangedDetail: The server reported different settings for this room than the ones its key was made for, so nothing was decrypted or sent. Ask the person who created the room for a new one.
whiteboard.about.1.title: How to start
whiteboard.about.1: Choose a room name, keep the generated passphrase or type your own of at least 16 characters that is hard to guess, and open the board. Send the link to your collaborators and share the password separately, ideally in person or over another app. The password is not part of the link.
whiteboard.about.2.title: Encryption
whiteboard.about.2: The password goes through Argon2id once, with 64 MiB of memory, 3 passes and a salt made from the room name, and HKDF-SHA256 splits the result into a base key and a separate value that lets you into the room without revealing the key to the server. Every stroke, shape, text and cursor movement is padded and encrypted in your browser before it leaves, each message with its own AES-256-GCM key derived from the base key and a fresh random salt, so even hours of busy cursor traffic never wear out a single key.
whiteboard.about.3.title: What the server sees and keeps
whiteboard.about.3: The relay on Cloudflare Workers passes encrypted updates between participants and stores nothing. The drawing lives only in the browsers of the people in the room and syncs between them as encrypted CRDT updates. When the last person leaves, the board is gone, so export a PNG if you want to keep it. The relay can see how many people are connected and when updates are sent, and Cloudflare sees IP addresses.
whiteboard.about.4.title: Good to know
whiteboard.about.4: Anyone with the room name and password can join and see everything on the board, so treat the pair like a key. Up to 32 people can draw together, and anyone in the room can lock it so that nobody new can join until they unlock it or leave. The board also has its own encrypted chat. Its messages travel with the drawing, so newcomers see recent ones and they vanish when the last person leaves; end a message with !N to make it disappear after N seconds.
whiteboard.about.5.title: Signatures and keys
whiteboard.about.5: Each browser also keeps its own signing key for every board. Everything you send, from strokes and cursor moves to chat messages, is stamped with the room, the time and a unique id and signed with that key before it is encrypted, so the relay cannot replay old updates and nobody in the room can speak under someone else's name. The first key seen with a name is trusted; if the same or a lookalike name later shows up with a different key, it is marked as a new key on the cursor and in the chat. Open the people list in the bottom bar to compare safety numbers and trust the key.
whiteboard.keyNewHint: This name was seen with a different key before. Compare the safety number in person before you trust it.
whiteboard.safetyNumberHint: Read a safety number out to the other person. It is the same on both screens and matches only when you both hold each other's real keys. A key code belongs to one key alone and tells apart two members with the same name.
whiteboard.boardMissing: This board does not exist yet, and the password is too weak to create it. Enter a stronger password or create the board on the setup page.

security.chat.title: Encrypted chat, calls, whiteboard, and files
security.chat.p1: Chat messages, typing indicators, and call signaling are encrypted in the browser (AES-GCM) before they reach the relay. The relay forwards ciphertext and does not store chat message history, except for saved rooms, where it keeps the encrypted messages (at most 1000 per room, in the European Union) until a member deletes the room or it has gone unvisited for 90 days. In rooms without server history, messages also have forward secrecy: each member's sending key moves on with every message and reaches the others only under keys from short-lived key pairs that are never stored, so recorded traffic stays closed even to someone who learns the password later.
security.chat.p2: Live calls use WebRTC with a TURN-only ICE policy so peer IP addresses are not exchanged directly. Besides DTLS-SRTP, every audio and video frame is end-to-end encrypted in the browser with AES-256-GCM (SFrame-style insertable streams, VP8 or VP9 for video). Each sender's media key is random, travels only inside the encrypted and signed room channel, is sealed again for each recipient with an ephemeral ECDH P-256 key, and is replaced whenever a participant leaves. Because media keys never pass through the DTLS handshake, recording call traffic now and breaking that handshake later, for example with a quantum computer, does not expose the media to anyone who lacks the room secret. Browsers without frame encryption cannot join calls. TURN credentials are fetched from encrypt.click (/api/turn).
security.chat.p3: Chat file attachments are encrypted in the browser before upload, the same way as in Encrypt & share. They go to our own storage and are deleted after 24 hours, even in saved rooms. When our storage is unavailable, the encrypted file goes to a public Send instance in the EU instead, where it can stay for up to 7 days.
security.chat.p4: New rooms always need a password of at least 16 characters that passes a strength check, and they can only be created through the create form. The password is never part of the link, so share it separately.

security.share.title: Encrypted message and file sharing
security.share.p1: Encrypt & share runs AES-GCM in your browser before anything is uploaded. The password stays on your device unless you copy or send it yourself.
security.share.p2: Automatic upload prefers first-party ciphertext storage (this site's /upload). That path is limited to about 90 MB and a monthly budget, and availability is guaranteed for about 24 hours. If it is full or unavailable, you are asked first; if you agree, your browser posts ciphertext only to encrypt.click's upload API, which relays it server-side to temporary Send-compatible hosts (files up to 50 MB). Those hosts should see ciphertext and server egress - not a direct browser upload of plaintext.
security.share.p3: Recipients open links on encrypt.click (often /u). Encrypted material may sit in the URL fragment (not sent to our servers on normal page loads) or point at uploaded ciphertext. Optional PNG wrapping can hide the share link in an image for offline handoff.
security.share.p4: Uploads are free, so automated or unusually heavy use is checked. Normal uploads go through without anything extra; when an upload looks automated or a device has uploaded a lot, the browser first has to solve a short proof-of-work puzzle. It runs on your device and involves no third party. Each further puzzle within the hour takes twice as long, and a solved one lets that device keep uploading for an hour, within the same hard daily limits.
security.chat.p5: Whiteboard sessions use the same realtime infrastructure for collaborative strokes and state. Treat room access like chat: use a strong password for anything sensitive.
security.chat.p6: Saved rooms use a random key carried in the link fragment, which never reaches the server. In every room, each message is signed in the browser with a per-room key, so other members can tell when a name turns up under a different key, and the message mode is bound into the room key, so the server cannot change it. Saved rooms add an ML-DSA-44 signature to every message and chain each author's stored messages, so browsers notice when the server leaves out, reorders or holds back messages.
security.network.li5: The deployment check compares freshly fetched assets and the build manifest from this server. It cannot prove the authenticity of the code running in your browser or protect against a compromised host.
